P1.evidence: The setter check was inverted — rather than reading anything back the rep asked the prospect to recount it, 'How was your call with Kim?', and accepted 'we just went over the general information' without probing. That single follow-up would have surfaced the expectation gap that killed the call. Frame was two-part plus alignment, missing what's in the way and what you need. No agreement question. Open question ran verbatim.

P2.evidence: Training history, diet and energy were all asked directly and well. Everything else was volunteered rather than gathered. Height and weight came out inside a goal question and age arrived twenty minutes later as an aside, 'I just turned 30' — neither was asked. Occupation surfaced at 00:14:00 during the mobility pitch, when the prospect mentioned he is an office worker sitting at a desk all day, and the rep did not pick it up. No health-conditions question at all, and no injuries question: the lower back pain was volunteered in the same breath, and duration, severity and whether he had seen anyone about it were never established. Sleep appeared inside the energy answer, unasked.

P3.evidence: Two good moves. The look-fit question was properly forked — 'some people it's like, I want to be super jacked, some people it's like, I want to be lean, what does that look like for you?' — and the bridge ran cleanly: 'you're on this call for a reason... what changed for you to make it more of a priority?' That produced the single richest line of the call, 'I just turned 30, and I've been on and off this train of me wanting to be fit, and I've just never reached this, so I just want to bite the bullet and say that I tried.' The rep then went no further. No 'what does that do for you', nobody else's stake, nothing on identity or what another decade of this looks like. The reflect-back was tactical rather than personal: 'you've kind of been shooting from the hip a little bit' — 'A lot.'

P4.evidence: The best root-cause work in the batch. The consistency pattern was diagnosed precisely with a forced choice — 'Is it more so, hey, I'll be all in for six months and then not go for three months? Or is it like, well, I kind of just go sometimes?' — and then pushed past the easy answer: 'Aside from the commute, what typically holds you back from being more consistent?' The gap was then named by the prospect in his own words after a clean elicitation, 'what do you feel like you really need?': 'Accountability and structure. I think the structure is probably going to be the most important because for the most part of my working out life, I've just been eyeballing it, free-balling it, no real 100% structure.' Only P4f is missing, and here the reframe was arguably unnecessary since the prospect had already located the problem in structure rather than information.

P5.evidence: Never ran, and it is the phase that would have decided this call. The prospect had just turned 30 and described a decade of starting and stopping — the exact setup for 'if nothing changes, what does this look like in two years' and 'is that something you're willing to settle for'. None of it was asked. The price then landed on a prospect who liked the method but had been given no reason for urgency, and he declined it in under a minute.

P6.evidence: No belief question and no all-in question. What the rep took as commitment was approval of a description: 'How do you feel about it in terms of process? Do you feel confident?' — 'it seems pretty straightforward. It seems really logical to me.' The all-in question is what would have surfaced the budget ceiling before the price rather than after it, and on a call where the prospect had arrived expecting a $200/month product it was the single most valuable question available.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and failed, so the phase is scored rather than marked not applicable. No payment collected, no onboarding call with Trevor booked, no agreement, no welcome sequence. The prospect left with a Skool link pasted into the Zoom chat and no commitment of any kind attached to it — no card taken, no follow-up, nothing scheduled, despite him saying he would 'for sure' sign up.

objection_plays.detail: The clearest money objection in the batch and the play did not run at all. 'A thousand bucks per month is pretty steep' and 'I don't got 6,000 bucks laying around' got a one-line value assertion — 'It's not supposed to be cheap, brother' — followed immediately by an unprompted offer to break up the payment. No isolation question, no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no permission to discuss finances, and not one of the six financial-picture questions: cash on hand, monthly surplus, number of cards, available credit, used versus available, investments. When the prospect said it was not an option the rep agreed in five words, 'Yeah, it's all good, dude', and moved to the downsell. Roughly ninety seconds elapsed between the price being named and the sale being abandoned.

'I'm just going to have to eventually just come back to you guys' is a deferral with no date attached. Nothing ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and no attempt to attach a date or a next step to the eventual return.

Script gap, and it is upstream of the rep. The prospect arrived with a materially wrong expectation of both the product and the price, having asked the setter directly and not been told: 'I did talk to Kim, and I did ask about the price, but you know, didn't really get any answer on that', and 'I was thinking that this program was going to be something kind of like a school thing, more of a group. I wasn't thinking of one on one.' There is no play for a prospect who has been mis-set, and no step in P1 that would catch it — the setter read-back is written as a rapport move rather than a qualification check. A single question at 00:00:59 about what Kim had told him about price and format would have redirected this call in its first minute.

notes: Strong discovery — the best P4 in the batch — attached to a prospect who could not buy and had said so to the setter before the call. Two coaching points, one for the rep and one for the process. For the rep: run P5 before the price, and when a money objection lands, isolate it and run the financial picture before conceding, because ninety seconds from first objection to abandoning the sale is not a play. For the process: the setter did not answer a direct price question, and P1a needs to become a qualification check that confirms what the prospect has been told about price and format, not just a rapport gesture.
